analysis.one_liner: Restores the 10-part-per-billion arsenic limit in drinking water that the EPA had proposed to withdraw.
analysis.headline: The bill to reinstate the tighter arsenic standard never left the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In its final days, the Clinton administration finalized a rule cutting the legal limit for arsenic in drinking water from 50 parts per billion to 10 parts per billion, the level used by the European Union, Japan, and the World Health Organization. The new Bush administration EPA proposed to withdraw the rule before it took effect. This bill would have put that rule back into force by law and locked the 10-part-per-billion limit in place unless Congress itself changed it. It was referred to the Senate environment committee and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 13 million people whose drinking water exceeds the old arsenic limit, who would get stronger protection against cancer and other health problems. Public water systems could tap the drinking water state revolving loan fund to help pay for treatment upgrades.

how_it_helps.text: Restores the EPA rule issued January 22, 2001, which lowers the permissible arsenic level in drinking water from 50 parts per billion to 10 parts per billion, giving it full force of law.
The rule's protections would cover about 13 million people against cancer and other health problems caused by arsenic in drinking water.

At the old 50-parts-per-billion limit, the National Academy of Sciences found drinking water 'could easily' carry a 1-in-100 cancer risk, and the bill notes that risk is 10,000 times the cancer risk EPA allows for any carcinogen in food.
The 10-parts-per-billion limit matches the standard already used by the European Union, Japan, and the World Health Organization.
Locks the 10-parts-per-billion limit in statute so it could not be weakened again by a future administration without an Act of Congress.
Public water systems facing treatment costs can apply for help through the drinking water state revolving loan fund, which had made about $3.6 billion available since 1996.

analysis.who_pays: Public water systems, especially smaller ones in areas with naturally high arsenic, which would bear the cost of treatment or new water sources, with costs likely passed to ratepayers. Federal loan funds would absorb part of the cost.

drawbacks.text: Water systems would face real compliance costs to meet the tighter limit, and smaller systems generally have fewer customers to spread those costs across; the bill itself points to the revolving loan fund as the offset, but loans still must be repaid.
The bill would fix the arsenic limit in statute, takeable away the EPA's ability to revise the number as new science comes in, allowing changes only through a new Act of Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health stakes are large: the bill's findings describe a cancer risk at the old limit that vastly exceeds what EPA tolerates for any carcinogen in food, and the new limit simply matches what Europe, Japan, and the WHO already use. The costs fall on water systems, with federal loan assistance available, though the rigidity of fixing the number in statute is a legitimate design criticism.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dodd introduced the bill on March 27, 2001, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
The bill's findings state that on March 20, 2001, the EPA administrator proposed to withdraw the arsenic standard finalized on January 22, 2001, before it took effect on March 23, 2001.
No further action was ever taken after the committee referral: no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, through the end of the 107th Congress on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Water systems facing the cost of meeting the tighter arsenic limit were better off in the short term, since the question of whether the stricter standard took effect was left to the administration rather than written into law.

for.name: Christopher J. Dodd
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate the 10-part-per-billion arsenic standard and lock it in statute.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no further action; no markup or committee vote was ever held, and the bill died in committee.

against.name: EPA under President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Proposed on March 20, 2001 to withdraw the arsenic standard finalized on January 22, 2001, creating the dispute the bill was written to resolve.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, but the bill never reached a vote, so the record shows no roll-call to measure the partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would force water systems to treat or replace water sources to meet a 10-part-per-billion arsenic limit, a cost that would flow to ratepayers; it offers federal revolving loan funds as partial relief. Water systems' interest in a looser standard runs against the health protection ordinary drinkers would get.
Systems with few customers and naturally higher arsenic levels face the steepest per-household compliance costs, since treatment plants cost the same whether they serve 500 people or 50,000.
